stated_availability: Appendix A (p.18): "Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921." In-text statements add: "The script used to run all validation analyses is available in the supplementary information" (p.4, §2.3.3) and "The script used to run all case study tests is available in the supplementary information" (p.8, §2.4). No dedicated data repository, DOI, or accession number is given for any dataset. Only aggregate summary statistics (mean/SD/min/max) for each case study are reported in-text (Tables 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7); raw individual-record morphometric data are not deposited by this paper. Readers are directed to original source publications for the case-study data (a mix of open-access journal articles, paywalled monographs, and one unpublished PhD thesis). The article itself is CC BY 4.0 open access (p.1).

barriers: The two core validation assemblages (replica handaxe n=500, replica archaic point n=45) are the authors' own newly created data with no repository deposition or data-sharing statement anywhere in the paper; the archaic point set is explicitly stated to be otherwise unpublished ('have not been used in any other published studies', p.4, §2.3.2) — co-author/author held.
Olduvai Bed IV cleaver data sourced from an unpublished PhD thesis (Martín-Ramos, C., 2022, University College London) — closed thesis, inaccessible.
Middle Historic ceramic bowl data sourced from Petrie (2020), a monograph (Oxbow Books) — typically paywalled/library-access only.
Neolithic Impressed Ware and Stentinello pot data sourced from Robb (2007), a monograph (Cambridge University Press) — paywalled.

Most case-study data are presented in this paper only as aggregated summary statistics (mean/SD/min/max per variable), not as the raw individual-record measurements that would be needed to actually rerun the OLE subsampling procedure, regardless of whether the cited source paper is itself open access.

No dedicated data repository, DOI, or accession number exists for any of the underlying morphometric datasets; the paper's own supplementary information is stated to contain only analysis scripts, not raw data.

F1.evidence: No DOI, IGSN, SWHID, or accession number is given for any dataset. Appendix A (p.18) points to 'https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921' — the article's own DOI, not a distinct data-record identifier.

F2.evidence: No standalone structured metadata (title/description/keywords for a deposited dataset) exists. The only structured metadata present belongs to the article itself (Keywords, p.1: 'Morphometrics; Incomplete record; Fragmentary data; Archaeological discovery; Lithics; Ceramics; Metals'); underlying case-study data appear only as in-text summary tables (Tables 1, 5, 6, 7) with no accompanying dataset descriptor.

F3.evidence: No identifier exists for any dataset (see F1), so no metadata record can include one.

F4.evidence: No mention anywhere in the paper of Zenodo, Figshare, DataCite, tDAR, ARIADNEplus, or any other searchable data registry; data reside solely within the Elsevier article/supplementary package.

A1.evidence: data_completeness coverage assessed as 'minimal' (~23%, 3/13 enumerated case-study/validation datasets). Per the A1 completeness rule this sets A1=0; no ethical-restriction exception applies (no CARE/human-subjects issue in this artefact-morphometrics paper).

A1_1.evidence: Article stated to be open access: 'This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)' (p.1), hosted on ScienceDirect and retrievable via standard HTTPS/DOI resolution, no paywall or login, for whatever material (in-text tables, supplementary information) is provided.

A1_2.evidence: No restricted-access or authentication/authorisation scenario is evidenced anywhere in the paper (no CARE, human-subjects, or other justified restriction), and no protocol capability for authentication is demonstrated; unscoreable, defaults to 0.

A2.evidence: The article carries a persistent Crossref-registered DOI (10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921) via an established publisher (Elsevier/ScienceDirect, Journal of Archaeological Science 162 (2024) 105921, p.1); this bibliographic metadata record would remain resolvable even if supplementary files became unavailable, per standard DOI-registry persistence.

I1.evidence: All case-study data are presented only as PDF-embedded summary tables (Tables 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7 giving mean/SD/min/max per variable), not in a structured machine-readable format (CSV/JSON/etc.); no structured data file is described anywhere.

I2.evidence: No controlled vocabulary, ontology, or FAIR-compliant terminology scheme (e.g. Getty AAT, CIDOC-CRM) is cited for describing artefact attributes; variable names (length, breadth, thickness, mass, elongation, refinement) are used descriptively without reference to a formal standard.

I3.evidence: Case-study datasets are linked to source publications only via ordinary narrative author-year citations (e.g. 'following the method outlined by de la Peña and Wadley (2014)', p.7), not as qualified, typed references (e.g. 'isDerivedFrom [DOI]') within a structured metadata record; no such record exists since no dataset metadata record exists (see F2).

R1.evidence: Case-study tables (e.g. Table 5, p.12) report a plurality of relevant attributes per dataset -- mean, minimum, maximum, OLE-estimated minimum/maximum, and percentage range extension for each morphometric variable (length, breadth, thickness, mass, etc.) -- giving reasonably rich description of what is shared.

R1_1.evidence: 'This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)' (p.1) -- a clear, machine-readable licence applied to the article and its associated content.

R1_2.evidence: Provenance is described for each case-study dataset -- source publication, collecting context and measurement protocol -- e.g. 'Data are derived from Buchanan and Hamilton's (2021) study of scaling laws in Paleoindian points... the methods used to collect [them]... are outlined in this study' (§2.4.1.5, p.6); 'the methods used to collect these data have been previously described in Martin-Ramos (2022)' (§2.4.1.3, p.7).

R1_3.evidence: Morphometric data collection follows established, cited domain protocols for lithic, ceramic and metal artefact measurement (e.g. handaxe methods 'described in Key and Lycett (2017)', p.4; Paleoindian points 'following Buchanan and Hamilton (2021)'; ceramics 'measured using diameter boards... callipers and a metal rule (see: Petrie, 2020)', p.8), consistent with community-standard archaeological measurement conventions.

F1.evidence: No DOI, SWHID, or accession number identifies the code; it is referenced only as 'the script' within the article's generic Appendix A supplementary-data link (same article DOI 10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921, p.18), not a dedicated software identifier.

F2.evidence: No structured software metadata (CodeMeta.json, CITATION.cff or similar) is mentioned; the code is described only in prose: 'The script used to run all validation analyses is available in the supplementary information' (p.4, §2.3.3) and 'The script used to run all case study tests is available in the supplementary information' (p.8, §2.4).

F3.evidence: No identifier exists for the code (see F1), so no metadata can include one.

F4.evidence: No mention of GitHub, Zenodo, Software Heritage, CRAN, or any searchable code registry; the script is bundled only within the generic Elsevier supplementary-data package.

A1.evidence: Both scripts (validation analyses and case-study tests) are explicitly stated to be included in the article's supplementary information, retrievable via the standard DOI/HTTPS resolution given in Appendix A (p.18: 'Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921'); the paper claims full script coverage of its own analyses ('all validation analyses', p.4; 'all case study tests', p.8).

A1_1.evidence: Retrieval is via the same open-access (CC BY 4.0, p.1), paywall-free ScienceDirect DOI link used for the whole article -- a standard, free, universally implementable HTTPS protocol.

A1_2.evidence: No authentication/authorisation mechanism, restriction, or justification is evidenced for the code; not demonstrated either way, defaults to 0.

A2.evidence: As for the data, the article's Crossref-registered DOI (10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921) with an established publisher provides a persistent metadata record independent of the continued availability of the supplementary script files.

I1.evidence: The code is an R script -- 'All analyses were undertaken in "R" version 4.3.0' (p.4, §2.3.3) -- a formal, shared, machine-parseable programming language, not an unstructured document format.

I2.evidence: No controlled vocabulary, ontology, or software-naming standard is referenced for the code.

I3.evidence: No qualified, PID-typed references to software dependencies (e.g. versioned package citations, DOIs for libraries used) are provided; only the bare R version number is given, without package-level citation.

R1.evidence: The methodology sections (§2.1-2.3, pp.2-4) document the algorithm and its parameters in substantial detail -- sampling percentages (5%, 10%, 20%, 50%), k values (5, 10, 20, 30), and iteration counts ('One thousand iterations of each process were performed', p.4) -- describing what the shared script implements, even though this lives in the article text rather than a dedicated code README.

R1_1.evidence: The CC BY 4.0 licence stated for the article (p.1) extends to the associated supplementary materials distributed through the same open-access mechanism; no separate/conflicting code licence is stated.

R1_2.evidence: Software-environment provenance is documented: 'All analyses were undertaken in "R" version 4.3.0' (p.4, §2.3.3), specifying the exact software version used.

R1_3.evidence: No evidence of adherence to software community standards (package structure, unit tests, CRAN submission, JOSS-style review, dependency lockfile); the code is described only as an ad hoc analysis script.
